During the receive cycle, the RXD line is normally HIGH and the falling edge on this line triggers the beginning of a received START bit. The USART removes the START, PARITY and STOP bits and READS the data to the display (DS2-DS9).
The experiment demonstrates asynchronous simplex data transmission. Whenever a data character is sent, the USART automatically adds a START, PARITY and STOP bits as selected in the mode instruction.

Prior to starting data transmission or reception, the USART must be loaded with a mode instruction control word generated by the CPU. This instruction defines the general operational characteristics of the USART.

The receiver ready (RXRDY) output from the USART goes HIGH to signify it has characters to receive. The RXRDY output is sent to U5A and U5B via S7B, S10 and S7A to control data reception.
The transmitter empty (TXE) output from the USART goes HIGH to signify it has no characters to transmit. The TXE output is sent to U5A and U5B via S7B, S10 and S7A to control data transmission.
The transmitter clock (TXC) and receiver clock (RXC) inputs to the USART, control the rate at which a character is transmitted and received.
The DSR and CTS inputs to U8 pins 22 and 17, simulate handshaking commands that allow serial data transfer. A CTS LOW input enables the USART to transfer serial data.
The chip select (CS) input on Pin 11 of U8, is held LOW to simulate the CPU enabling the USART to READ and WRITE.

The CPU control/data (C/D) input to the USART, is simulated by switch S6. The C/D, WR and RD inputs combine to define the word on the data bus as either a data character, control word, or status information. 1 = CONTROL 0 = DATA
The WRITE (WR) "LOW" input to the USART, signifies the CPU is writing data or control words out of the USART.
S7A and S7B simulate CPU control and mode selection inputs to the USART. The READ (RD) "LOW" input to the USART, signifies the CPU is reading data from the USART.
IC1 is a voltage regulator for the 12 VDC and +5 VDC power to the circuit card.
The RS-232-C interface is accomplished by feeding the TXD and RXD lines from and to a line driver and receiver SN75155 (U1).
12 VDC referenced to ground provides the required voltage for MARKs and SPACEs.
The CLOCK circuit U6, provides an input to the USART to generate internal device timing and to multivibrator U5 to control READ and WRITE inputs.
The RESET circuit U3A, sends a HIGH to the USART upon power on and re-initialization. The HIGH places the USART in an "idle" mode until a control word is written into the USART program.
The external Baud Rate Generator is demonstrated by the Baud Rate Manual Clock S2, and the Baud Rate Settings S3. U6 provides selectable baud rates ranging from 300 to 9600 bits per second (BPS).
PC130-232 card switches will be used to demonstrate CPU control of the USART. S5, U4, U7 and DS2 - DS9 represent the data bus, data and input control and data bus display.
DATA INPUT
We are using simplex communication with primary handshaking. Handshaking is demonstrated by the use of switches S8 (CTS) and S9 (DSR).
Notice we are using internal connections on the Nida Model 130E Trainer and PC-130-232 cards to simulate our cable.
PC-130-232 pin T, is the TXD line and pin E is the RXD line.
Remember UART's and USART's perform four functions in the RS-232-C line interface. Convert parallel signals to serial for transmission and converts serial in parallel during reception.
Adds start, parity and stop bits during transmission and removes them during reception.
Computes the parity bit on transmitted and received
Convert parallel signals to serial for transmission and converts serial to parallel during reception.
Computes the parity bit on transmitted and received characters and reports detected errors.
Sets up the appropriate handshaking signals and reports the status of incoming handshaking circuits.

The circuit you will analyze in the experiment uses RS-232-C electrical characteristics. Asynchronous serial data transfer will be demonstrated by the USART 8251 chip with an external baud rate generator.
The RS-232-C line interface is the worldwide accepted standard for serial data communications.

The receiver ready (RXRDY) output from the USART goes HIGH to signify it has characters to receive. The RXRDY output is sent to U5A and U5B via S7B, S10 and S7A to control data reception.
The transmitter empty (TXE) output from the USART goes HIGH to signify it has no characters to transmit. The TXE output is sent to U5A and U5B via S7B, S10 and S7A to control data transmission.
The transmitter clock (TXC) and receiver clock (RXC) inputs to the USART, control the rate at which a character is transmitted and received.
The DSR and CTS inputs to U8 pins 22 and 17, simulate handshaking commands that allow serial data transfer. A CTS LOW input enables the USART to transfer serial data.
The chip select (CS) input on Pin 11 of U8, is held LOW to simulate the CPU enabling the USART to READ and WRITE.

The CPU control/data (C/D) input to the USART, is simulated by switch S6. The C/D, WR and RD inputs combine to define the word on the data bus as either a data character, control word, or status information. 1 = CONTROL 0 = DATA
The WRITE (WR) "LOW" input to the USART, signifies the CPU is writing data or control words out of the USART.
S7A and S7B simulate CPU control and mode selection inputs to the USART. The READ (RD) "LOW" input to the USART, signifies the CPU is reading data from the USART.

Polling is a cycle of; examining status, reading, examining status, reading, examining status and so on. Polling requires the sender and receiver to use the same baud rate to prevent data loss between cycles.
The UART processes data through a cycle of examining and reading the internal status register. Each time a character is read, the register is reset for the next character to be examined.

The UART contains several internal memory locations called registers. They hold the latest character received, the next character to transmit, the current status of handshaking signals, send and receive information about the chip.
Typical UART connections consist of parallel data transfer, TXD/RXD, clock signal, DTR/DSR, I/O circuitry, interrupt lines to the CPU and a chip select pin that directs the chip to function.

Pins 12 through 24 are not used often. They provide secondary functions for more complex serial data transfers.
Pins 8 and 22 are MODEM lines. Pin 8, is Carrier Detect (CD). Pin 21, is the Ring Indicator (RI), and responds to the telephone ringer.

Pins 4 and 5 are secondary handshaking lines. Pin 4 is Request to Send (RQS) and Pin 5, Clear To Send (CTS). The receiver requests data transfer, and the transmitter responds with clear to shift when ready.

Pins 6 and 20 are primary handshaking lines. Pin 6, Data Set Ready (DSR) indicates the transmitter is ready to send data. Pin 20 Data Terminal Ready (DTR) indicates the receiver is ready to receive data.
Pin 2 Transmitted Data (TXD) carries the transmitted data signal and Pin 3 Receiver Data (RXD) carries the received data signal.
Pin 1 is a protective ground (PG) or chassis ground. Pin 7, signal ground (SG), is a ground reference for all other pins.

By using handshaking, the computer will stop sending data when the printer gets behind. Then, when the printer is ready, the computer sends more data.

Handshaking is used to control the flow of serial data between the transmitter and receiver before, during, and after its transfer. It also prevents two devices from transmitting at the same time.

The RS-232-C interface dedicates specific lines for input and output device handshaking. On these lines the SPACE's mean the line is ON or ready to receive. MARK's mean OFF or stop not ready to receive.
